items.title: Working at worship, worshipping at work: approaching material, practice, and value
items.abstract: This article analyzes the intersections between work and worship in the ancient Mediterranean from an archaeological perspective and provides an introduction to this special section. The goal is to challenge and move beyond two conceptual frames that have been deeply persistent in scholarship on the ancient world: (1) the imposition of two distinct category-containers “religion” and “work,” which we contend have been constructed and held separate due to particular idealist, capitalist, and colonialist ways of conceptualizing the past; (2) notions of the “embeddedness” of ancient religion, which we argue rarely acknowledge the underlying Polanyian economic baggage. We propose taking an explicitly relational and praxeological approach, drawing on notions of “lived religion” that, unlike the prevalent model of “Lived Ancient Religion,” often consider the intersections of production and worship, and focusing on the ways practices, spaces, materials, persons, and divine powers articulate in particular constellations.

items.title: Chytra rituals in Athens
items.abstract: This essay examines the use of an ordinary household item – a chytra (stewpot) – to ritual effect. It focuses on Classical and Early Hellenistic deposits under the floors of a single room of the Classical Commercial Building, just north of the Athenian Agora. The plan of the building and workshop debris found in its floors identify it as a workplace, and the repeated appearance of the chytra and its orientation and relationship to the stratigraphy and other objects constitutes evidence of the ritual practices of those who worked there. Ancient texts and other chytra deposits, both in this building and elsewhere in the excavation, throw more light on these practices, constituting evidence for “religion-as-lived” in the Athenian workplace.

items.title: A Vesta’d interest: apotropaia and shrines as vernacular risk management strategies in Vesuvian bakeries
items.abstract: Pompeian commercial and industrial shrines are often cursorily lumped into the monolithic category of lararia , obfuscating their complexity. The shrines’ diverse combinations of deities, playful iconographies, and spatial placements suggest complex and dynamic strategies of appropriation and bricolage. Contextualized reassessment of assemblages and features reveals remnants of creative, “vernacular” ritual action. I argue that Pompeii’s pistrina proprietors prioritized familiar, locally invested deities alongside or even instead of the Lares to create a more personal, accessible space in their commercial ventures for reciprocal interaction with the divine – most notably, a variation of Vesta and her donkey. Spatial choices also indicate preferential construction of shrines in spaces that were particularly risky, with many closely associated with the mouth of the oven. But shrines were just one tool in a wider protective arsenal deployed around the volatile oven, which included amuletic and apotropaic interventions.

items.title: A fishy business at Pompeii: the House of the Sarno Lararium
items.abstract: The House of the Sarno Lararium at Pompeii (I.14.7) is known for the enigmatic scene painted on the lararium in its rear courtyard. Following a common practice in classical archaeology of identifying an artistic scene based on a reference in an ancient text, it has been interpreted as documenting the arrival of onions. This article proposes a novel interpretation. I argue that the scene represents a group of fishermen bringing their catch back to port, weighing it, and preparing it for distribution. To support this interpretation, I show how the imagery on the lararium can be linked to fishing and the pictured deity, Sarnus. Employing theoretical concepts of “taskscapes” and “lived religion,” I argue that this scene of non-elite fishermen indicates how household worship was entangled with daily labor, as well as how daily labor took place against the backdrop of a ritual landscape.

items.title: Wielding the axe, tending the priestly ornaments: religious labor in the emperor’s household
items.abstract: This paper investigates the ritual labor performed by the enslaved and freed members of the familia Caesaris who supported the emperor in his role as priest. Drawing on Roman art and funerary inscriptions, it contrasts elite and non-elite perspectives regarding religious work. Visual depictions – such as reliefs of the Ara Pacis and imperial sacrifice scenes – frame attendants as anonymous extensions of the emperor’s ritual authority, performing physical and sensory tasks that enhanced his prestige but denied their individuality. In contrast, inscriptions from the familia Caesaris record victimarii , musicians, and custodians of sacred implements who chose to highlight these roles in funerary commemoration. Their job-titles signaled skill, training, and membership in social networks that extended beyond imperial service, including participation in collegia and communal tombs. Examining these sources together reveals how ritual work was simultaneously devalued by elites and deeply meaningful to its practitioners, shaping identities, communities, and the lived experience of Roman religion.

items.title: Face of Ancient Andean Man Reconstructed
items.abstract: PUNÍN, ECUADOR—Live Science reports that the face of a man who lived in Ecuador's Andes […] The post Face of Ancient Andean Man Reconstructed appeared first on Archaeology Magazine . PUNÍN, ECUADOR— Live Science reports that the face of a man who lived in Ecuador's Andes Mountains some 3,000 years ago has been digitally reconstructed by Christopher Rynn. The man’s skull, known as Punín-2, was discovered in a ravine in the Chimborazo region of Ecuador in the 1970s. Rynn explained that the man descended from an ancestral group of North Siberians and East Asians. “Punín-2 resembles an East Asian skull from the front, but not at all from the side,” he said. Physical analysis of the skull suggests the man was about 50 years old when he died. Rynn used digital techniques, partial physical reconstruction with wax, and data on the thicknesses of tissues to recreate the face. He also consulted with people who now live in the Chimborazo region—and are likely to be descended from Punín-2—for guidance on the hairstyle and the setting of the eyes in the reconstruction. “The hairstyle is very specific,” Rynn said. “If it’s wrong, it looks like a different tribe,” he explained. items.abstract: We have, says Simon Sebag Montefiore, long needed a history of the modern Middle East encompassing all the myriad peoples, forces and states that have shaped the region. That’s why, he tells Charlotte Vosper, he decided to brave the heat of The Cauldron Charlotte Vosper: You begin your new book with Abdulaziz’s raid on Riyadh in 1902, a major event in the foundation of Saudi Arabia. Why? Simon Sebag Montefiore: Virtually all histories of the Arab world start with the traditional Levant – Jerusalem, Lebanon, Syria – or Constantinople; anywhere but Saudi Arabia. Yet Saudi is really the centre of the Middle East. The holy cities of Mecca and Medina are in Saudi Arabia, so the Gulf has become the heart of the Arab and Islamic worlds. I began my book with Riyadh to signal that this is very much an Arab-centric history of the modern Middle East. Plus I think that Abdulaziz Ibn Saud’s raid is one of the best stories – like something out of Lawrence of Arabia . What powers were at play there at the turn of the 20th century? items.title: Scandinavian Aurochs: Still Alive 6,500 Years Ago
items.abstract: Ancient DNA, 108 radiocarbon dates and Mesolithic bone piles suggest hunting, inbreeding and spreading forest together ended the Scandinavian aurochs. Two aurochs bones from Scania, in the far south of Sweden, were sequenced a second time for a paper in The Holocene , 1 which raised their coverage to 1.19X for the animal called Ska1 and 2.18X for Ska3. That was enough to read their runs of homozygosity, the stretches where the copies of a chromosome inherited from each parent are identical. Counting only runs longer than a megabase, the totals came to 918 megabases for Ska1 and 917 for Ska3, a near tie between two animals that were not necessarily contemporaries. No other aurochs in the comparison set carries as much uniform DNA, including the Sicilian animal, the Jutland animal, and every mainland European and British genome the team lined up beside them. Most people who know the aurochs know how it ended: the last cow died in a Polish forest in the 17th century, and people did it. The authors accept that for Poland. Radiocarbon dating places the burial between A.D. 1450 and 1500, which means the leaves stayed in that wool for more than five centuries, in a site on Peru’s south coast where the climate is dry enough to keep fragile plant tissue intact. items.title: Inka scattered sacred coca leaves over sacrificed llamas, excavation suggests
items.abstract: Deep in Peru's Acarí Valley lie the ruins of Tambo Viejo, an Inka provincial center where excavations have uncovered tasseled sacrificial llamas and brightly adorned guinea pigs. But save for a few seeds and some stored leaves, evidence of how the Inka used one of their most sacred plants in rituals remained elusive. Now, archaeologists have discovered coca leaves still stuck in the wool of some sacrificed llamas.

items.title: First Americans: DNA Lineages No Older Than 21,000 Years
items.abstract: Ancient DNA from 1,204 people in the Americas shows lineages diversifying no earlier than 21,000 years ago, an awkward fit for the oldest sites. The oldest human genome recovered from the Americas came out of a Clovis burial site in western Montana, from a child known as Anzick-1 who died about 12,800 years ago. Nothing older has been sequenced from either continent, which means that every genetic argument about when the first Americans arrived is built on people who lived later, with the earlier events inferred from statistical models fitted to their DNA. About 257 whole genomes and genome-wide data from 1,204 ancient individuals have now been published for the hemisphere, and the review that tallies them (Bethany Potter and Jennifer Raff of the University of Kansas, with Savannah Hay and Archana Singh, in Current Opinion in Genetics & Development , 1 2026) is frank that this is still a thin and uneven sample. Most readers who follow the field carry a tidy story about it. items.title: Flat Head Syndrome in 42% of Iron Age Italians
items.abstract: Skulls from Matelica, Italy, show deformational plagiocephaly nearly 3,000 years before the Back to Sleep campaign Eleven skulls from two cemeteries at Matelica, a town in the Marche region of central Italy, are flatter at the back than they should be, and on one side more than the other. Most are flattened on the right. The people who owned them were buried in the mid-ninth to eighth century BCE, in deep rectangular pits at the necropolises of Crocifisso and Brecce, and the shape of their heads is the same one pediatricians now measure with calipers and 3D imaging in infants who sleep in the wrong position. The condition is deformational plagiocephaly, or flat head syndrome, and the team led by Michael Allen Beck De Lotto of the University of Padua found 1 it in 11 of the 26 crania preserved well enough to assess, or 42.3%. items.title: 20th-Century Railroad Worker Camp Found in Iowa
items.abstract: SIOUX CITY, IOWA—Siouxland Public Media reports that traces of a worker camp have been uncovered […] The post 20th-Century Railroad Worker Camp Found in Iowa appeared first on Archaeology Magazine . SIOUX CITY, IOWA— Siouxland Public Media reports that traces of a worker camp have been uncovered at the Sioux City Railroad Museum by a team led by Michael Betsinger of the University of Iowa Office of the State Archaeologist. Workers lived on site to build the Milwaukee Railroad Shops Terminal from 1916 to 1918. The repair shop terminal served the Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Paul and Pacific Railroad. More than 500 people were employed at the repair shop and its roundhouse of 30 stalls during World War II. But when the railroad began to use diesel engines in the 1950s, the repair shop became obsolete. The Siouxland Historical Railroad Association acquired the property in 1995 and reopened it as a museum. To read about immigrant railroad workers in the American West, go to " America's Chinatowns: Labor ." Early medieval sculpture fragments from Lios Mòr LISMORE, SCOTLAND— The Independent reports that traces of an early Christian monastery have been found on the small Scottish island of Lios Mòr, or Lismore, by a team of archaeologists and community volunteers. Local tradition, evidence from the place name, and historical records indicated that a monastery had been built on the island in the sixth century A.D. by Saint Mo Luóc. It was not clear, however, if a later cathedral had been constructed on the site of the early monastery, or if it was located somewhere else, said Clare Ellis of Argyll Archaeology. items.title: Inside Venice’s Jewish ghetto
items.abstract: Historian Alexander Lee explores why, in the early 16th century, Venice confined its Jewish population to a restricted quarter on an island in the city In the early 16th century, Venice confined its Jewish population to a restricted quarter on an island in the city. It was the first settlement to bear the name 'ghetto' – a word that would go on to shape the history of Jewish persecution and segregation. Speaking to Emily Briffett, historian Alexander Lee explores why Venice created the ghetto, examining the uneasy tension between the city’s economic reliance on Jewish money-lenders and its deep suspicion of Jewish residents. He also reveals what life was like inside the ghetto, from its crowded buildings and religious institutions to its vibrant cultural life, intellectual debates and fragile relationship with the Venetian authorities.

items.abstract: East of Eden tells the story of two families, the Trasks and Hamiltons, and traces the impact of “psychic monster” Cathy Ames on their lives. But how true is the new Netflix series to Steinbeck’s epic tale – and California in the 19th and 20th centuries? Jonathan Wright investigates Published in 1952, John Steinbeck regarded East of Eden as his greatest novel. “It has everything in it I have been able to learn about my art or craft or profession in all these years,” he later said. Primarily set in the Salinas Valley in California, it follows the story of two families: the Trasks and the Hamiltons. Steinbeck took the title of the book from the Book of Genesis. He explores the novel’s themes – love, depravity, moral courage, the way our lives are shaped by those who go before and the choices we make – with reference to the story of Cain and Abel, the sons of Adam and Eve. Playing out over seven episodes, the Netflix version of East of Eden has space to explore these weighty themes. The 600-year-old bronze weapon measures about nine inches long and weighs about two pounds. Engravings on the handle record the weapon’s name, weight, manufacturing supervisor, craftsman, and an incomplete date. items.title: Homo erectus in South Africa: Outnumbered 10 to 1
items.abstract: A skull fragment from Drimolen pushes the adult Homo erectus record back to 2 million years ago, among far more Paranthropus. The fossil catalogued as DNH 127 came out of a loose, partly decalcified block of breccia on the southeast side of the DNH 7 Pinnacle, in the old lime-mining pit at Drimolen Main Quarry, about forty kilometres northeast of Johannesburg. The excavation records give the year as 2008. It is a right temporal bone with a piece of parietal and a scrap of occipital attached, the part of the skull behind and above the ear; the parietal wall above the suture stands 44.7 millimetres tall and is at most 7.2 millimetres thick. Nobody described it for years. Now Jesse Martin, of the Palaeoscience Labs in the Department of Archaeology and History at La Trobe University, and four co-authors have assigned it, tentatively, to Homo erectus . That makes it the first adult of the species from Drimolen, and at roughly 2.04 to 1.95 million years old it predates the adult Homo erectus fossils from Dmanisi in Georgia, which are about 1.8 million years old. a. items.abstract: Michael Wood on unlikely characters in the Bayeux Tapestry's story I first saw the Tapestry in the old Bibliothèque municipale in Bayeux, almost a lifetime ago now. Its magical power is all the more poignant because it was made by English needlewomen as a record of the brutal conquest of their own land – a defeat so harrowing that it took a century for the English to accept. Some would say they never did. The Bayeux Tapestry, it’s now agreed, was made in England, probably at Canterbury. Its English sympathies are among its many extraordinary aspects. It tells the tale of the noble hero who fatefully broke his oath – an oath that by tradition was sworn at Bayeux. There are 626 people depicted on the Tapestry, with just three women – one of them nameless and clutching her child’s hand as her house is burned down and she flees in terror. Of the men who are named, most are kings, dukes and bishops, the key characters in the story. But there are three exceptions that have always intrigued historians. Turold, Wadard and Vitalis are three of the Norman rank and file. Why are they on the Tapestry? That question leads us directly to the matter of who commissioned it, and why. Read more | In…

items.abstract: Babylonian scribal schools taught religion through god-lists, and at Uruk the priests trained on them used the lists to raise Anu above Ištar. In 202 BCE, in the southern city of Uruk, an administrator named Anu-uballiṭ (Kephalon, in the Greek name he also used) renovated a temple to the sky god Anu and had bricks stamped with an inscription saying the building had been raised by Adapa, the sage who lived before the flood. The temple, called Bīt Rēš, was not ancient. Another member of his family, also named Anu-uballiṭ and known in Greek as Nikarchos, had built it in 244 BCE, forty-two years earlier, and the scribes who wrote the brick inscription handled the temple’s earlier building history with the same techniques found in older royal inscriptions, which they were able to read because Babylonian scribes were trained on such texts. items.title: REDISCOVERING THE DEAD: REANALYSIS OF A LOST IRON AGE CEMETERY AT HIGHSTED, KENT
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, EarlyView. Summary Highsted, near Sittingbourne in Kent, was the location of a large cemetery, thought to date to the Late Iron Age. The site was excavated under rescue conditions in 1955, but due to the apparent theft of the archive and finds, was never published. As part of a wider project, the human remains have been subject to new osteological examination, ancient DNA (aDNA) and isotope analysis, and AMS dating. Alongside this, the surviving finds have been reassessed, and the excavation pieced together from contemporary photographs and newspaper records. Analysis revealed a burial population which spanned the Late Iron Age and early Romano‐British periods, with continuity into the second century AD and possibly beyond. Burial rites echo those from the nearby site of Mill Hill, Deal, confirming Highsted as a major Deal‐rite cemetery. Despite Continental parallels for these types of burials, the Highsted population grew up in the local area, with homogeneous diets including some marine resource exploitation, reflecting the dietary impacts of the Roman conquest on indigenous rural communities. items.title: 489 Spear Points Show Clovis Newcomers Wasted Less Stone
items.abstract: In Tennessee’s chert-rich river valley, the first Ice Age hunters resharpened their points to stubs while Cumberland successors discarded usable ones. In the Tennessee River Valley, countless small drainages have cut down into four chert-bearing rock formations, the Fort Payne, the Warsaw, the St. Louis and the Ste. Genevieve, and left the stone lying in tabular slabs and cobbles along their beds. Chert breaks like thick glass, and it is the stone Ice Age knappers in the region worked into spear points. The two archaeologists behind a new study of the valley’s earliest artifacts describe its supply as effectively limitless, which makes it odd that the first people known to have lived there, the makers of Clovis points, used it as though it might run out. Jesse Tune, director of the Center for Archaeological Research, examines a replica of a Cumberland spear point, one of two types of stone projectiles he and Shane Miller, assistant professor of anthropology at the University of Alabama, studied to gain insights into the lives of ancient inhabitants of the Tennessee River Valley. items.title: Teotihuacan Writing Was Real: 3 Glyphs on a Mexican Cliff
items.abstract: Red glyphs painted in Cave 19 at Chalcatzingo, Morelos, name a Singing Mountain and add new evidence that Teotihuacan had a true writing system. On the western face of Cerro Delgado, a 110-metre hill of volcanic rock in the Mexican state of Morelos, there is a rock shelter that nobody can walk to anymore. The team that recorded it in August 2022 climbed the hill from its gentler eastern side and abseiled down the cliff, and they suspect that in antiquity people reached it from below on scaffold-like ladders, using footholds that someone chipped into the steeper stretches of rock. Archaeologists call it Cave 19, though it barely qualifies as a cave: it is 5.43 metres wide and at most 2.24 metres deep, and the lip of rock overhead hangs between 1.46 and 1.85 metres above the floor, low enough that a tall visitor stoops. At the back, above a bedrock shelf blackened by old fire, someone sometime between the fourth and sixth centuries AD took a brush and dark red pigment, probably haematite, and painted three designs. items.title: Robot wars in the classroom: why AI in education is nothing new
items.abstract: As the role of AI in education sparks debate, Laura Tisdall examines past technological advances in teaching, and how they were received at the time In 1929, the British magazine Teachers World identified ‘A Possible Menace to the Free Development of Education’. The putative culprit was BBC Radio, which had begun its schools broadcasting programme five years earlier, provoking fears that teachers would simply become ‘machine minders’. Such concerns pre-dated radios, though. The first ‘teaching machines’ were developed in the US in the 19th century; it was claimed that they could, for example, teach students to spell by getting them to turn a crank to arrange letters in the correct order. items.abstract: When he was captured by the Nazis in 1944, George Lascelles – the eldest nephew of King George VI – became one of Colditz Castle’s most important prisoners. David Lascelles tells the remarkable story behind his father’s time in captivity, and why, decades later, he decided to track down a pistol belonging to the man who let his father walk free It was April 1945. As the Second World War entered its final stages, my father, First Lieutenant George Lascelles of the Grenadier Guards, was imprisoned in Oflag IV-C, Colditz Castle . The prisoners there called it a straflager – a punishment camp – much to the irritation of their German captors, who insisted it was just an ordinary PoW camp but with better security. It was where they sent particularly troublesome prisoners, the habitual escapers and those considered to be deutschfeindlich , hostile to German ways. My father, just 22 years old, didn’t see himself as any of those. He had been a prisoner for less than a year and had never tried to escape. What he was, though, was well connected. His maternal uncle was King George VI , and he was one of a small group of young British officers being held together in Colditz, all of them related…

The pit was roughly kidney-shaped and held the bones of at least three people, and those bones had been moved around inside it: the skulls gathered in the southeastern corner, most of the rest piled toward the middle, several long bones laid along the western wall. Göbeklitepe (the older two-word spelling, Göbekli Tepe, is still the more common one in English) lies 15 kilometers northeast of the city of Şanlıurfa in southeastern Türkiye, and for the first two decades after excavation began in 1995 it was described as a sanctuary: a place where hunter-gatherers came together to raise T-shaped pillars carved with wild animals, and where hardly anyone lived. items.title: Are these history's greatest losers? 19 people who had glory snatched away from them
items.abstract: History may celebrate the winners, but what about those who came tantalisingly close to the top spot? Jonny Wilkes shines a light on 19 famous ‘almosts’ At the 2026 London Marathon, Kenya’s Sabastian Sawe made history by becoming the first runner ever to finish the 26.2 miles in under two hours, breaking the tape with a time of 1:59:30. While the crowd cheered and the commentators tried to capture the significance of the moment, another runner, Yomif Kejelcha of Ethiopia, quietly passed the finish line too, and also under two hours. While still a remarkable achievement, it is doomed to be overshadowed by Sawe – and all for the sake of 11 seconds. Second place, the silver medal, the so-called ‘first loser’: it can be a heartbreaking position, to be so close and yet so far from the ultimate glory. (Before you feel too bad for Kejelcha, though, it is worth noting that this was his first-ever marathon, so imagine what he could accomplish with more training.) Whether in the field of exploration, invention, politics or sport, history is replete with examples of close-but-no-cigar runners-up, although their names don’t fill as much space in the history books as the ones who pipped them. items.title: Scientists discover the first diplodocus ever found outside North America
items.abstract: A 150-million-year-old dinosaur fossil from Spain has been identified as the first confirmed Diplodocus ever found outside North America. items.title: WHAT ONCE WAS SHALL BE AGAIN: PALAEOLITHIC BIFACES AT THE NEOLITHIC SITE OF GIV'AT RABI EAST
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, EarlyView. Summary Giv'at Rabi East is a Pre‐Pottery Neolithic B site located in northern Israel, interpreted as a flint workshop. One area has been spatially identified as a ‘biface locality’; it is characterized by the presence of finished axes and preforms alongside débitage. Interestingly, Acheulean bifaces have also been recovered from this area. Aside from these, no other diagnostic Lower Palaeolithic artefacts have been identified, and the integrity of the Neolithic contexts is well established. It is therefore suggested that Neolithic knappers collected Acheulian bifaces from nearby sites and brought them to the workshop. Technological similarity along with an apparent appreciation for artefacts knapped hundreds of thousands of years earlier – and for the ancient people who knapped them – may partially explain this intriguing phenomenon. These findings shed new light on the enduring significance of bifacial tools in the lives of Neolithic communities in the southern Levant.

items.title: A sharper picture of a pandemic: Uncovering the complex history of the plague after the Black Death
items.abstract: The Black Death is often remembered as a single catastrophic event that swept across Europe between 1347 and 1353, killing millions. Yet the disease did not disappear after that first devastating outbreak. For more than four centuries, plague continued to return in recurring waves, reshaping communities, economies and societies across Europe and beyond. A new study led by researchers at the University of Tartu sheds fresh light on this long and complex history by analyzing the DNA of the plague bacterium preserved in archaeological human remains. The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

items.title: Ancient DNA: Coastal and Inland Finns Were One People in 1250
items.abstract: Genomes from 34 Iron Age and medieval burials show how Swedish migration after 1250 reshaped Finland’s southwest coast while inland Häme barely changed. Sometime between 1031 and 1147, a woman was buried at Laukskola, a cemetery on the Daugava River in Latvia. Her community probably spoke Liv, a Finnic language that has nearly died out, and its grave goods are rich enough that archaeologists tie its wealth to the trading places along the river. Her genome, already published, turns up in a new analysis with long stretches of DNA that match two people buried in Finland in roughly the same period. One was buried at Raisio, on the edge of Turku near the southwest coast. The other was a parent buried at Mikkola, in the inland municipality of Ylöjärvi, at the same site as three of that parent’s children. The amount of DNA involved puts both relationships at sixth cousins or more distant, implying an ancestor some generations back who crossed between Latvia and southwestern Finland in one direction or the other. items.title: FROM SCANDINAVIA TO THE LEVANT: THE LATE BRONZE AGE METAL TRADE AND NURAGIC SARDINIA
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, EarlyView. Summary A growing body of evidence suggests that Nuragic Sardinia played a role, as yet poorly understood, in the metal trade between Scandinavia, Atlantic Europe, and the Mediterranean during the Bronze Age. Provenance studies based on lead isotope and chemical analyses of copper‐based – and to a minor extent lead – artefacts from both continental Europe and the Mediterranean indicate that metals of Sardinian origin were exported and used in different and far apart regions over the second half of the second millennium BC. This noticeable flow of metals from Sardinia appears associated to distinct counter‐flows of Nuragic pottery both to the east and to the west of the island. Breaking down the chronology of such movements unveils specific distribution patterns over different phases of the Bronze Age. By critically assessing such patterns, this paper discusses how the study of Nuragic Sardinia may contribute to a refined understanding of the complex interplay between the socio‐political transformations that characterize Bronze Age Europe and what must have been a permanent demand for metal.

items.title: MINDING THE GAP: A METHODOLOGICAL AND CHRONOLOGICAL REASSESSMENT OF EASTERN MEDITERRANEAN PURPLE‐DYE PRODUCTION IN THE BRONZE AND IRON AGES
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, EarlyView. Summary Purple dye was an iconic status symbol in the ancient Mediterranean, yet tracing the expansion and shift of production from the Aegean to the Levant encounters substantial methodological difficulties. Using Tel Shiqmona – a unique industrial centre with a continuous Iron Age sequence – as an archaeological benchmark, this study defines detailed and granular criteria for identifying production. Applying these criteria reveals a 300‐year ‘gap’ (c.950–650 BC), when Shiqmona remains the sole site with significant production evidence. This paper argues the gap represents a consolidation: a shift from dispersed crafts into centralized, state‐controlled production, first attested at Shiqmona in the ninth century BC. By providing a chronologically sensitive database for the Levant, this study lays foundations for examining broader Mediterranean‐wide trajectories. The centralized and specialized production attested at Shiqmona offers a plausible template for understanding the industry’s seventh century BC resurgence in the Levant, as the wider adoption of the ‘Shiqmona model’ under Neo‐Assyrian hegemony.

items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, EarlyView. Summary This article examines the settlement systems and spatial organization in the Upper Tigris region during the Pre‐pottery Neolithic (PPN), based on data from recent rescue excavations and ongoing systematic fieldwork. The approach focuses on location preferences, covering valleys, river terraces, and water sources. Settlement layouts and scale, and the spatial distribution of communal areas are considered in relation to household practices. Evidence from neighbouring regions, particularly the Middle Euphrates basin, is briefly contemplated to provide a comparative background. The available data demonstrates that the Early Neolithic settlements in the Upper Tigris region generally developed within valley settings. They were characterized by a dispersed, multi‐centred pattern, suggesting locally variable ways of handling settled life.

items.title: MIDDLE IRON AGE V‐SHAPED PRECIOUS METAL FINGER‐RINGS IN BRITAIN
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, EarlyView. Summary The first V‐shaped finger‐ring reported from Britain was a silver specimen found in 1921–26. No more came to light until discoveries of gold examples by metal detectorists from 1997 onwards. There are now ten such gold rings from Britain, a third of the European total. There is no trail of these gold rings known between their Central European homeland and the English Channel, making those in Britain a distinctly anomalous phenomenon. They first appear c.400 BC in Austria‐Slovakia. Their popularity peaked at the end of the fourth and in the early third centuries BC. Afterwards, there was a steep decline, and they were not made at all later than c.200 BC. Although none from Britain has a context or definite associations, they can be proposed as ritual offerings of jewellery worn by elite women. Their currency in Britain spanned the period between the first arrivals of continental gold torcs and the development of insular schools of gold jewellery.

items.abstract: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

items.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
items.abstract: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

items.title: Protect fossils from hammer-wielding tourists | Letter
items.abstract: Jill White responds to an editorial calling for fossils to be given legally protected national-treasure status I write this while sitting on Charmouth beach in Dorset with my required reading of the Saturday Guardian, as I do regularly. Your editorial ( The Guardian view on the export of fossils: they deserve national treasure status, 21 August ) produced a hollow laugh as – this being the centre of fossil hunting on the Jurassic Coast – I am surrounded by armies of hammer-wielding tourists busy smashing the daylights out of any rock available around them. The vast majority have no idea which stone types are likely to bear fossils and don’t report any finds even if they are lucky. Others take carrier bags full of stones back to their cars. Thus, we have no idea what fossils are being lost to the record every single day here, and so I completely support the suggestion of giving them legal protection. Of course, amateur collecting has a valuable place in unearthing important fossil finds, but only if they are shared and documented. The Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre valiantly tries to educate and inform visitors, but sadly these will inevitably be the minority. Continue reading...

items.abstract: Ancient fossils suggest insects conquered land through a long amphibious phase rather than making an abrupt jump from water to dry ground. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

items.abstract: Miocene South America was packed with giant prey—and the predators hunting them were just as spectacular. Fossil bite marks suggest crocodylians, especially the enormous Purussaurus neivensis, were more important predators than mammals in this ancient tropical ecosystem. At around seven meters long, Purussaurus may even have helped control populations of giant herbivores.

items.title: 16 mummies and a dog reveal a hidden order inside an ancient Egyptian tomb
items.abstract: A tomb in Egypt’s Theban Necropolis reveals a surprisingly organized story of burial, reuse, and changing beliefs spanning hundreds of years. Researchers found 16 mummified people, the remains of at least four more, and a mummified dog, with burials ranging from wealthy individuals laid in coffins with amulets and imported goods to later bodies carefully stacked in increasingly crowded spaces.

items.title: Olga Soffer obituary
items.abstract: Professor of anthropology whose approach to archaeology centred on crafts executed by women 40,000 years ago Olga Soffer, who has died aged 83, brought a revolutionary idea into the conversation about prehistoric ice age people: women mattered. Inspired when working on archaeological excavations in the former USSR, and by remains from a dig in Moravia, in the 1990s she presented a case for women as makers of textiles, baskets and nets, critical to survival in bleak northern conditions 30,000 years ago. Her achievement was the more remarkable for her career path. By then a professor of anthropology at the University of Illinois, she had obtained her three degrees over three decades, partly while also working as a cosmetics buyer and fashion promoter for a New York department store. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

items.title: Scientists find evidence for two origins of life on Earth
items.abstract: Scientists probing life’s deepest origins have uncovered evidence that the first free-living cells may have emerged not once, but twice. The findings suggest a striking possibility: life may share one ancient genetic code, yet have undergone two separate transitions into free-living existence.

items.abstract: A forgotten fragment of a lost papal letter is offering a surprising new explanation for the Norman Conquest. England may have backed the wrong pope during a bitter religious power struggle, giving Pope Alexander II a political reason to support William the Conqueror’s invasion. The discovery suggests Harold’s downfall in 1066 was shaped by intrigue in Rome as well as bloodshed at Hastings.

items.title: 240-million-year-old reptile fossil reveals a lost chapter before dinosaurs and crocodiles
items.abstract: A 240-million-year-old reptile discovered in Brazil is revealing what evolution looked like just before the rise of dinosaurs and crocodiles. The small predator had unusually positioned legs that may have allowed it to move more efficiently than many earlier reptiles. Its close relatives were previously known mostly from other continents, suggesting these ancient animals spread much farther across the Triassic world than scientists realized.

items.abstract: Discovery of 2,100-year-old vessel hailed as ‘one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years’ A 2,100-year-old Roman shipwreck carrying about 500 amphorae has been discovered 3 miles off the coast of Mazara del Vallo in Sicily. Italy’s Carabinieri cultural heritage protection squad investigated the wreck with the help of divers and underwater cameras after receiving a tip-off from fishers. The vessel was found at a depth of about 46 metres (151ft) and was carrying hundreds of amphorae – ancient two-handled ceramic jars with a narrow neck – thought to have been used mainly to transport wine. items.title: For 15,000 years, humans and dogs have been changing each other
items.abstract: Dogs have been shaping—and being shaped by—humans for about 15,000 years, evolving from early partners of hunter-gatherers into an astonishing range of specialized companions. Across the globe, they adapted alongside people to wildly different environments and needs, from powerful Arctic sled dogs and agile rainforest hunters to high-altitude dogs with genetic traits for surviving thin air. Some were even bred for wool, while others played important spiritual or ceremonial roles.

items.title: Dinosaurs became giants — so why did they never become tiny?
items.abstract: Dinosaurs conquered the land at enormous sizes, but strangely, they almost never evolved into truly tiny animals. New research suggests that physiology alone can’t explain this missing miniature end of the dinosaur spectrum—and that early mammals may have been partly responsible. While dinosaurs kept mammals from becoming large, small mammals may have returned the favor by occupying ecological niches that could otherwise have supported mouse-sized dinosaurs.

Detailed brain reconstructions show that Tametara mirim was adapted for burrowing, while another ancient snake was suited to life above ground. Other fossils point to marine lifestyles as well. By 80 million years ago, snakes were already experimenting with very different habitats and sensory systems.

items.title: This 4,000-year-old city defied the rules of history
items.abstract: As Mohenjo-daro prospered, the gap between its richest and poorest households actually shrank. Its shared infrastructure, fair trade systems, and lack of powerful royal elites suggest that equality may have helped fuel the ancient city’s success.

items.title: A forgotten fossil just revealed a new Triassic predator from 210 million years ago
items.abstract: A fossil overlooked for nearly 80 years has revealed a previously unknown crocodile relative that lived 210 million years ago in what is now New Mexico. Named Eosphorosuchus lacrimosa, the jackal-sized predator had a reinforced skull, powerful jaw muscles, and a short snout built for tackling larger prey.

But throughout August, English Heritage is offering visitors the chance to win some guaranteed solitude within the hulking stones. Continue reading...

items.title: Hidden charcoal reveals the true age of ancient cave paintings
items.abstract: A new analysis has precisely dated paintings in France’s Font-de-Gaume cave for the first time. Scientists discovered charcoal inside black pigments once thought to contain only minerals, allowing them to use radiocarbon dating. The results show that a bison was painted about 13,000 years ago, while sections of a mask-like figure were added during several widely separated periods.

items.title: The Guardian view on ancient DNA: a female shaman exposes our flawed assumptions about the past | Editorial
items.abstract: Thanks to new technology we are are acquiring insights into earlier times, and realising how little we truly know Archaeologists believe the Upton Lovell Shaman, who lived in what is now Wiltshire 4,000 years ago, was an important religious leader and metalworker because of the artefacts and tools buried with the body. Until very recently it was also believed, on considerably slimmer evidence, that this shaman was a man: it was simply assumed that someone of such status must be male, and the view was barely questioned over the years. Now ancient DNA analysis performed at the Francis Crick Institute has revealed that the body, held by the Wiltshire Museum, is in fact a woman. That should cause a stir in bronze-age studies. But it is also yet another example of how many of our assumptions about human history have been upended by the rise of ancient DNA analysis over the past two decades. items.abstract: Early humans in England crafted a rare piece of elephant bone into a reusable hammer for sharpening stone tools nearly 500,000 years ago. The extraordinary find reveals that ancient toolmakers were resourceful, skilled, and capable of surprisingly advanced planning.

items.title: Ancient ape fossil in Egypt challenges the story of human origins
items.abstract: A newly identified fossil ape from northern Egypt is reshaping ideas about where the ancestors of modern apes first emerged. Analyses place it closer to living apes than any known East African species of the same age, pointing to North Africa and the Middle East as a possible birthplace and crossroads for the ape lineage that eventually produced gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, and humans.

items.title: New giant salamander species discovered in 3.5-million-year-old fossils
items.abstract: Fossils discovered in Japan more than two decades ago have finally been identified as a new genus and species of giant salamander. Limnospondylus ajimuensis lived around 3.5 million years ago in a warmer, wetter Kyushu and may have reached 1.1 meters in length. Its discovery hints that many more unknown giant salamanders could be hiding among fossils previously given the wrong classification.

items.title: Ancient ferns turned Triassic Europe into a wildfire inferno
items.abstract: Ancient fern savannahs may have transformed parts of Europe into a wildfire-prone inferno during the end-Triassic mass extinction. New fossil evidence suggests the ferns repeatedly regrew after fires, creating fresh fuel that helped prolong the devastation.

items.title: Ancient DNA reveals a chilling secret at China’s 4,000-year-old Shimao city
items.abstract: Ancient DNA from China’s vast 4,000-year-old Shimao settlement is revealing how one of East Asia’s earliest complex societies was organized. Researchers found that its people were largely descended from local Yellow River farming communities, but also had genetic ties to distant southern and steppe populations, pointing to extensive prehistoric contact.

items.title: Scientists just discovered a lost branch of Australia’s marsupials
items.abstract: Fossils from Queensland suggest a newly recognized marsupial order may have survived in Australia for around 35 million years, rewriting part of the story of how the continent's unique mammals evolved. The discovery challenges the idea that Australia's marsupials all came from a single straightforward ancestral lineage.

items.title: Origins and features of Early Roman priesthoods: literary sources, images and material culture
items.abstract: This paper examines three early Roman priesthoods, specifically, the Vestal virgins, the Salii, and the Flamines, through the lens of their visual and symbolic prerogatives, adopting a diachronic perspective based on literary sources, iconographic evidence, and archaeological data. The study highlights the deep historical roots of priestly paraphernalia in pre- and proto-historic funerary contexts, as well as a significant shift in gender dynamics. Prior to the 8th c. BCE, numerous male religious and martial figures are depicted with double shields and other distinctive attributes. From the 8th c. BCE to the Archaic period, both male and female religious figures appear, often equipped with knives, while double shields gradually disappear. This pattern suggests an expanding definition of religious and political prerogatives. By the 8th c. BCE, specialized male and female figures (identified by their knives) assume religious roles, whereas male warriors become kings ( reges ), holding political authority and often serving as Augurs as well. *

items.title: Archaeologists found Homer's Iliad inside a 1,600-year-old Egyptian mummy
items.abstract: A 1,600-year-old mummy discovered in Egypt has revealed something archaeologists had never seen before: a fragment of Homer’s Iliad used during embalming. The papyrus was identified as part of the famous "Catalogue of Ships," one of the best-known sections of the ancient epic. Researchers say it is the first archaeological evidence of a Greek literary text being intentionally incorporated into the mummification process, adding a fascinating new chapter to the history of both literature and ancient burial customs.

items.title: Not just a housekeeper: a new look at the work of the Roman vilica
items.abstract: The presence of the vilica or female supervisor at a Roman villa is attested across five centuries in varied texts, and her duties are detailed in an entire book of Columella’s On Agriculture . This paper challenges assumptions by modern scholars that her managerial functions were confined to those of a housekeeper, focused on food supplies for the household and the supervision of domestic labor inside the house. Through closer examination of textual, iconographic, and archaeological evidence, we can see that the vilica ’s principal role was to oversee not the domestic sphere, but rather a range of vital productive activities on the farm. In particular, she seems to have been responsible for wine and oil making and for important rituals linked to production. This has implications for our understanding of the roles of women within Roman farming and the Roman economy.

items.title: Scientists finally solved the mystery of Earth's greatest mass extinction
items.abstract: Why do beaches today have seashells from clams and snails instead of brachiopods? A new study suggests the answer lies in Earth's greatest mass extinction, when warming oceans and falling oxygen levels wiped out animals that couldn't adapt. Species with body plans and metabolisms better suited to the changing conditions survived and went on to dominate the seas, offering a glimpse of how modern marine life could respond to climate change.

items.title: The Neanderthal “love story” isn’t what the DNA actually shows
items.abstract: Claims that Neanderthal men "preferred" Homo sapiens women may make for catchy headlines, but the underlying research does not actually show prehistoric romance. The genetic evidence only points to an uneven pattern of DNA inheritance, which could have been shaped by biology, migration, or social organization. Archaeological evidence suggests Neanderthal groups may have followed traditions where women moved between communities, opening the door to far more complicated explanations than simple attraction.

items.abstract: Scientists discovered ancient wolves on a tiny Baltic island where they could only have been brought by humans, suggesting an unexpectedly close relationship between people and wolves thousands of years ago. Evidence indicates the wolves were fed, possibly cared for, and may even have been managed or selectively bred long before modern ideas of domestication.

items.title: A STEP IN STONE. ONTOLOGIES OF PODOMORPHIC PETROGLYPHS IN SOUTHERN SCANDINAVIAN BRONZE AGE
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, Volume 45, Issue 3, Page 330-348, August 2026. Summary During the Bronze Age, a particular type of podomorphic petroglyph was produced on the outcrops by the sea in southern Scandinavia. In this text, their distribution, organization and articulation are analyzed in the Mälaren region of central‐eastern Sweden. The study shows that the petroglyphs are organized in relation to water as well as to different minerals visible in the rock. This pattern indicates that they are not simply images or symbols but also physical ‘devices’, produced to do something. It is argued that one purpose was for the frequent single podomorphs to be paired with another at a later stage. Because podomorphs in a pair generally are of different sizes and form, it is suggested that each one belongs to an individual of different age and/or sex – potentially depicted in stone to show existing or desired future relations, agreements, pacts, friendship, marriages etc.

items.title: QUANTIFYING THE SUPPLY OF ROMAN WINE AND OLIVE OIL IN FRANCE: AN AORISTIC ANALYSIS OF AMPHORAE ASSEMBLAGES
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, Volume 45, Issue 3, Page 349-368, August 2026. Summary This article analyses the dynamics of Roman olive‐oil and wine production and commerce in present‐day France from the second half of the second century BC to the mid‐fourth century AD, drawing on a corpus of more than 7000 amphorae recovered from Gallic and Romano‐Gallic settlements across the French territory, excluding Alsace. The methodology consists of a quantitative strategy based on aoristic distribution, assessing both regional and chronological trends according to production and settlement chronologies. The results highlight a clear preponderance of Italic wine in Late Republican Gaul, followed by imports from Hispania, before local Gallic wine came to dominate the domestic market and expanded to other provincial contexts. In parallel, the study traces initial Italic olive‐oil imports to southern Gaul, subsequently supplanted by the predominance of Hispanic oil and the growing presence of North African products. items.title: OLD SEALS NEW STORIES: THE COPPER AGE–EARLY BRONZE AGE STONE STAMP SEALS AND SEALING PRACTICES FROM ALİŞAR HÖYÜK
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, Volume 45, Issue 3, Page 306-329, August 2026. Summary This study examines 13 stone stamp seals excavated from the Copper and Early Bronze Age levels at Alişar and currently housed in the Museum of Anatolian Civilisations at Ankara (Türkiye). Through detailed documentation, typological analysis and comparison with sealing traditions in Anatolia and neighbouring regions, it explores their formal, iconographic and cultural characteristics. The seals demonstrate transcultural distribution patterns, reflecting intensified interregional interactions in the latter half of the Early Bronze Age. In particular, serpentine seals – similar in form to metal examples – are thought to have been burnished and used as alternatives to metal ones. It is also suggested that these stone seals may have been produced by local artisans. The Alişar seal assemblage reveals a synthesis of local and external influences and likely fulfilled both administrative and symbolic functions. By systematically presenting the typological diversity of the Alişar seals, this study sheds light on the cultural dynamics and interregional connections of Anatolia during the Early Bronze Age.

items.title: BRINGING BACK FAMILIAR FORMS: RECYCLING QUINA SCRAPERS AT THE LATE LOWER PALAEOLITHIC QESEM CAVE, ISRAEL
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, Volume 45, Issue 3, Page 250-277, August 2026. Summary This study presents a technological analysis of 18 old patinated scrapers and spalls, mostly of Quina technology, that were recycled into new scrapers of the same type at the Late Lower Palaeolithic site of Qesem Cave, Israel (420–200 kyr). Recycling scrapers into the same Quina and demi‐Quina types offers a rare, controlled opportunity to investigate a technology’s biographical character. Comparing the tools’ pre‐ and post‐recycling phases demonstrates that the selection of old items was highly intentional, guided by the original tool’s morphology and the affordances of its pre‐existing features. This process suggests an enacted perceptual experience, demonstrating a skilled recognition of the potential remaining in discarded objects. A sophisticated understanding of material properties and technological trajectories is thus revealed. This behaviour suggests a form of historically‐aware material engagement, offering new insights into the cognitive and technological capabilities of Late Lower Palaeolithic humans and providing a basis for future cognitive studies.

items.title: ARROWHEAD OR SPEARPOINT? EXPERIMENTAL ANALYSIS OF IMPACT TRACES ON SLOTTED BONE POINTS WITH MICROBLADE INSETS
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, Volume 45, Issue 3, Page 278-305, August 2026. Summary Slotted bone points likely originated in Palaeolithic traditions and evolved into efficient, reusable Mesolithic hunting weapons optimized for reliability and increased bleeding, reducing the risk of hunting failure. Such bone points were long debated as either spear tips or arrowheads, but earlier interpretations lacked reliable criteria. A newly conducted experiment show they function effectively as arrowheads when mounted on appropriate shafts and fired with bows of realistic Mesolithic draw weight. Damage patterns on bone points and insets matches archaeological finds from Motala in south‐central Sweden. Microblade durability varied with the inset raw material, though penetration did not. The type of adhesive had minimal effect on performance. The design’s main advantage lies in its long cutting edges, which create larger wound channels than plain bone points.

items.title: CONNECTIVITY AND CHANGE: GLAZED POTTERY NETWORKS IN THE MEDIEVAL EASTERN MEDITERRANEAN (ELEVENTH–FOURTEENTH CENTURIES AD)
items.abstract: Oxford Journal of Archaeology, Volume 45, Issue 3, Page 369-393, August 2026. Summary This paper investigates the economic and political transformations of the Medieval Eastern Mediterranean (late eleventh to mid‐fourteenth centuries AD) through the lens of material culture and Social Network Analysis (SNA). Using the distribution of seven types of glazed pottery as archaeological indicators, the study examines changing patterns of connectivity and the structural positions of sites within regional exchange systems. By applying SNA to presence/absence datasets, the analysis reconstructs the topology of interaction networks revealing a shift from a Byzantine‐centred system to one increasingly shaped by Italian maritime powers and the Crusader States, with the events of 1204 marking a critical turning point. Interpreted within a world‐systems perspective, the results trace the relocation of core functions from Byzantine centres to Italian city‐states, while highlighting the resilience of long‐established hubs within the reconfigured system.

items.title: Patronage and public amenities in Roman Epirus: the well of Junia Rufina at Butrint
items.abstract: The well of Junia Rufina has long been one of the main features of the archaeology of Roman Butrint. This paper aims at offering a chronological and cultural context for its dedication by inserting it into contemporary urban and historical developments. The monumentalization of the well in the 2nd c. CE illustrates how increased access to and architectural display of water was a main aspect of urban policy in the newly founded province of Epirus, in line with the rest of the Greek world. The role of Rufina, on the other hand, can be understood in the light of the cultural policies of the time, and as a manifestation of the power and prestige attached to female patronage in highly networked families throughout the Empire at the time of Hadrian.

items.title: Recent Trends in Archaeological Predictive Modeling and Automatic Structure Detection
items.abstract: Comparative review of recent developments in archaeological predictive models and automatic structure detection Mathias Bellat, Amy Hatton, Jordy D. Orellana Figueroa https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20610648 Recommended by view This paper was originally presented at the 2025 Computer Applications and Archaeology conference in Athens, Greece. In this paper, the authors have done an excellent job of comparing the recent literature on archaeological predictive modeling (APM) v. automatic structure detection (ASD). Boards and pieces survive in abundance, but the rules and conventions that animated them have vanished. The dominant tradition has filled this gap through comparison with better-documented games and close reading of fragmentary texts (Schädler, 1998; Finkel, 2007). Productive as this has been, it tends to assume that a game has a single recoverable ruleset, rather than a living practice continuously renegotiated by its players. items.title: A monumental apsidal building of the Roman Imperial period in Doliche
items.abstract: Excavations in the city center of the ancient city of Doliche in southeast Türkiye have brought to light the remains of a monumental apsidal building. Although the structure is poorly preserved due to looting and spoliation, the results of three seasons of excavation allow for an initial analysis and preliminary reconstruction. This article presents the building for the first time and discusses its importance in improving our understanding of monumental urban architecture in the region. The building is interpreted as a temple, and the article explores its potential links with apsidal temples in southern Syria and the Roman imperial cult.

items.title: The supply of metals in the later Roman Empire: framing the question
items.abstract: Whether the later Roman Empire ran short of precious or base metals, either at the level of the state or in private life, is a question that can only be answered in a tentative fashion. Surveying the period from the mid-2nd to the mid-7th c., this article weighs the difficulties presented by the full range of material and textual evidence, while attempting to establish a balance between all regions of the Roman world. It concludes by suggesting that there probably were indeed crises of metal production at certain periods, caused by the depletion of usable ores and hypothetically by a shortage of fuel.
